Build a small multi-user chat in the current working directory: a Python
backend on aiohttp, a plain JavaScript frontend, and an automated test for
it. A checker will start your server, talk to it over WebSocket, and drive
the page in a headless browser like a real user (typing and clicking).
Follow the contract below exactly.

## Files

- `server.py`
- `static/index.html`
- `static/app.js`
- `static/style.css`
- `test_chat.py`

## Server (`server.py`)

- Python 3 with aiohttp. It is started as `python3 server.py` from the
  working directory and must keep running until it is killed.
- Port: the `PORT` environment variable, default `8765`. Listen on `0.0.0.0`
  or `127.0.0.1`: the checker connects to `127.0.0.1`.
- `GET /` returns `static/index.html`. Every file in `static/` is also served
  at `/static/<name>`, and `index.html` loads `/static/style.css` and
  `/static/app.js` from there.
- The WebSocket endpoint is `/ws` on the same port.

## Protocol

Every WebSocket message is a text frame holding one JSON object.

Client to server:

- `{"type": "join", "nick": "<nick>"}`
- `{"type": "message", "text": "<text>"}`

Server to client:

- `{"type": "history", "messages": [...]}`: sent only to the client that
  joined, right after its `join`. `messages` holds the last 50 chat messages,
  oldest first, each in the `message` form below. System notices are not
  part of the history.
- `{"type": "system", "text": "..."}`: sent to every joined client when a
  client joins and when a joined client leaves (its WebSocket closes). The
  text names the nick, e.g. `alice joined`, `alice left`. Whether the joining
  client also receives its own join notice is up to you.
- `{"type": "message", "nick": "...", "text": "...", "ts": <number>}`: when a
  joined client sends a message, the server broadcasts it to every joined
  client, the sender included. `nick` is the sender's nick, `ts` is the
  server time in Unix milliseconds.

A client that is connected but has not joined gets no broadcasts, and its
`message` frames are ignored.

## Page

- `static/index.html` has elements with exactly these ids: `nick` (text
  input), `join-btn` (button), `msg` (text input), `send-btn` (button),
  `messages` (the chat feed).
- No auto-join. Loading the page must never send `join` by itself, not even
  with a default or remembered nick: the user joins only by acting. Until
  then `#nick` and `#join-btn` are visible and enabled, and `#messages` is
  empty (no placeholder text).
- Clicking `#join-btn` joins with the nick typed into `#nick`. Pressing Enter
  in `#nick` does the same.
- After joining, `#msg` and `#send-btn` are visible and enabled (before
  joining they may be hidden or disabled). Pressing Enter in `#msg` or
  clicking `#send-btn` sends the typed text as a message.
- On join, `#messages` shows the received history. After that, every
  incoming `message` and `system` notice is appended to `#messages` with its
  text visible. A message is shown when its broadcast comes back from the
  server (the sender receives its own broadcast too).
- The page may open the WebSocket on load or when the user joins.
- Plain JavaScript: no frameworks, no build step, nothing loaded from the
  internet. The checker's browser can reach only your server.

## Test (`test_chat.py`)

Write your own automated test and ship it with the code:

- It runs as `python3 test_chat.py` from the working directory, needs
  nothing already running, and finishes within 60 seconds.
- It starts `server.py` itself as a subprocess (use `sys.executable`), with
  `PORT` set to a free port it picks, waits until the server accepts
  connections, and stops the server at the end, also when a check fails.
- It checks the protocol with real WebSocket clients: join and history,
  broadcast between two clients, join and leave notices, history for a
  newcomer.
- It exits with status 0 only if every check passed, non-zero otherwise.

## Environment

`python3` on your PATH has aiohttp available. It is the same Python the
checker uses to run `server.py` and `test_chat.py`, so there is nothing to
install. Do not install packages globally. You may start the server and run
your test while you work, but you don't have to. Stop any server you started
before you finish.

## What counts as a finding

Report only problems that can actually break something:

- bugs: wrong logic, off-by-one, wrong comparison or operator, wrong value returned;
- broken contracts: code does not do what its doc comment, comment, name or caller expects;
- panics on reachable paths: `unwrap`/`expect` on fallible input, out-of-bounds indexing, integer overflow, division by zero;
- concurrency problems: races, deadlocks, locks held across `.await`, lost cancellation;
- leaked resources: files, child processes, tasks or channels that are never closed, killed or awaited;
- errors silently swallowed where the caller needs them;
- test gaps: new or changed behavior with no test covering it (this project requires tests with every change).

Do NOT report: style, formatting, naming, wording of comments or docs, "could be more idiomatic", refactoring ideas, performance guesses without evidence, or problems in code the diff did not touch. A diff that only edits comments or docs has no findings unless the new text contradicts the code.

## How to work

- The diff is the primary input. Paths in it are relative to the repository root; drop the `a/` and `b/` prefixes. The `read` and `grep` tools resolve paths against the repository root.

- Read only what you need to confirm or reject a concrete suspicion, usually just the changed files. Do not explore the repository. To find callers, definitions or tests, search with `grep` (a regex, optionally narrowed by `path`) instead of reading files at random. To list files or find one by name, call `grep` with `files_only: true`: the regex then matches file paths. If a search and one or two reads do not settle a suspicion, drop it and move on.

- Call tools silently: write no text before or between tool calls. Everything you write is shown to the user as the review.
- Report each defect once: a wrong line of code and the comment next to it are one finding, not two.
- Every finding must be backed by code you have actually seen. If you cannot confirm a suspicion, drop it. An empty list of findings is a good, valid result: never invent a problem to justify a verdict.

## Severity

- `blocker`: breaks the build or existing tests, panics or corrupts data on a normal path, or opens a security hole.
- `major`: a real bug on a plausible path, a broken contract, or new behavior without a test.
- `minor`: a real but low-impact defect.

## Output format

Your whole answer is the findings list followed by the verdict line. No preamble, no summary of the diff, no code blocks, no explanations outside the findings. List at most 10 findings, most severe first, one per line:

# Kanban board web app

## Brief

Build a small kanban board web app in the current directory: an aiohttp
backend, a plain JavaScript page and an automated test. The board has three
columns, To Do, Doing and Done; cards can be added, moved between columns and
deleted, and the board is kept in a JSON file, so it survives a restart.

## Requirements

### Server

- `server.py`, on aiohttp, started as `python3 server.py`.
- Port: the `PORT` environment variable, default `8770`.
- Serves the page at `/`.

### JSON API

- `GET /api/cards` returns the list of all cards. A card is an object
  `{"id": ..., "title": ..., "column": ...}`: the id is unique, the column is
  `todo`, `doing` or `done`.
- `POST /api/cards` with `{"title": ...}` creates a card in `todo` and returns
  it. A blank title: 400.
- `PATCH /api/cards/<id>` with `{"column": ...}` moves the card and returns it.
  An unknown column: 400.
- `DELETE /api/cards/<id>` removes the card.
- `PATCH` and `DELETE` answer 404 for an id that does not exist.

### Storage

- Every change is saved, before the server answers, to a JSON file at the
  path from the `BOARD_FILE` environment variable, default `board.json`.
- No file yet means an empty board.
- The board survives a restart of the server, even a hard kill.

### Page

- Plain JavaScript: no frameworks, no build step, nothing loaded from the
  internet.
- A text input `#new-card` and a button `#add-btn` that adds a card with the
  typed title. Pressing Enter in the input does the same.
- Column elements `#todo`, `#doing` and `#done`, holding one `.card` element
  per card.
- Each `.card` shows its title and has the buttons `.move-left` and
  `.move-right` (move it to the neighbouring column; they may be missing or
  disabled where there is none) and `.delete`.
- The page changes the board only through the API, loads it when it opens and
  always shows it exactly as the server stores it.

### Test: `test_board.py`

- Starts `server.py` itself as a subprocess on a free port with its own
  temporary `BOARD_FILE`.
- Checks the API.
- Stops the server, even when a check fails.
- Finishes within 60 seconds and exits 0 only if everything works.
- You run it and make it pass.

### Environment

- `python3` on your PATH already has aiohttp: install nothing.
- Stop the servers you started before you finish, each by the PID of the
  process you launched — never by matching names with pkill or killall: other
  processes on this machine are not yours.

   `BOARD_FILE`, the four API routes with their 400 and 404 answers, a save on
   every change.

# Multi-user WebSocket chat

## Brief

Build a small multi-user chat in the current working directory: a Python
backend on aiohttp, a plain JavaScript frontend and an automated test. Users
open the page, join under the nick they type and exchange messages over a
WebSocket; a newcomer sees the recent history. A checker will start your
server, talk to it over WebSocket, and drive the page in a headless browser
like a real user (typing and clicking). Follow the requirements below exactly.

## Requirements

### Files

- `server.py`
- `static/index.html`
- `static/app.js`
- `static/style.css`
- `test_chat.py`

### Server: `server.py`

- Python 3 with aiohttp. It is started as `python3 server.py` from the working
  directory and must keep running until it is killed.
- Port: the `PORT` environment variable, default `8765`. Listen on `0.0.0.0`
  or `127.0.0.1`: the checker connects to `127.0.0.1`.
- `GET /` returns `static/index.html`. Every file in `static/` is also served
  at `/static/<name>`, and `index.html` loads `/static/style.css` and
  `/static/app.js` from there.
- The WebSocket endpoint is `/ws` on the same port.

### Protocol

Every WebSocket message is a text frame holding one JSON object.

Client to server:

- `{"type": "join", "nick": "<nick>"}`
- `{"type": "message", "text": "<text>"}`

Server to client:

- `{"type": "history", "messages": [...]}`: sent only to the client that
  joined, right after its `join`. `messages` holds the last 50 chat messages,
  oldest first, each in the `message` form below. System notices are not part
  of the history.
- `{"type": "system", "text": "..."}`: sent to every joined client when a
  client joins and when a joined client leaves (its WebSocket closes). The
  text names the nick, e.g. `alice joined`, `alice left`. Whether the joining
  client also receives its own join notice is up to you.
- `{"type": "message", "nick": "...", "text": "...", "ts": <number>}`: when a
  joined client sends a message, the server broadcasts it to every joined
  client, the sender included. `nick` is the sender's nick, `ts` is the server
  time in Unix milliseconds.

A client that is connected but has not joined gets no broadcasts, and its
`message` frames are ignored.

### Page

- `static/index.html` has elements with exactly these ids: `nick` (text
  input), `join-btn` (button), `msg` (text input), `send-btn` (button),
  `messages` (the chat feed).
- No auto-join. Loading the page must never send `join` by itself, not even
  with a default or remembered nick: the user joins only by acting. Until then
  `#nick` and `#join-btn` are visible and enabled, and `#messages` is empty
  (no placeholder text).
- Clicking `#join-btn` joins with the nick typed into `#nick`. Pressing Enter
  in `#nick` does the same.
- After joining, `#msg` and `#send-btn` are visible and enabled (before
  joining they may be hidden or disabled). Pressing Enter in `#msg` or
  clicking `#send-btn` sends the typed text as a message.
- On join, `#messages` shows the received history. After that, every incoming
  `message` and `system` notice is appended to `#messages` with its text
  visible. A message is shown when its broadcast comes back from the server
  (the sender receives its own broadcast too).
- The page may open the WebSocket on load or when the user joins.
- Plain JavaScript: no frameworks, no build step, nothing loaded from the
  internet. The checker's browser can reach only your server.

### Test: `test_chat.py`

Write your own automated test and ship it with the code:

- It runs as `python3 test_chat.py` from the working directory, needs nothing
  already running, and finishes within 60 seconds.
- It starts `server.py` itself as a subprocess (use `sys.executable`), with
  `PORT` set to a free port it picks, waits until the server accepts
  connections, and stops the server at the end, also when a check fails.
- It checks the protocol with real WebSocket clients: join and history,
  broadcast between two clients, join and leave notices, history for a
  newcomer.
- It exits with status 0 only if every check passed, non-zero otherwise.

### Environment

- `python3` on your PATH has aiohttp available. It is the same Python the
  checker uses to run `server.py` and `test_chat.py`, so there is nothing to
  install. Do not install packages globally.
- You may start the server and run your test while you work. Stop the servers
  you started before you finish, each by the PID of the process you launched —
  never by matching names with pkill or killall: other processes on this
  machine are not yours.
